content_title: As measles cases continue to surge, are Pittsburgh schools prepared?
content: President Donald Trump just issued an executive order on how the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine should be administered to children. Measles, which was eliminated from the United States in 2000, has seen a resurgence as vaccination rates have declined . And as parents prep to send their kids back to school , cases are climbing in Pennsylvania, according to state data . While Allegheny County has no reported cases of measles, health officials are urging parents to vaccinate their children against the disease before they head back to the classroom later this month. Here's what to know about vaccination rates in schools throughout the county. Pittsburgh area school vaccination rates During the 2025-2026 school year, 93.8% of all students in Allegheny County were fully vaccinated, according to a report from the county's health department. Among the unvaccinated, 0.4% had medical exemptions, 2.2% had religious exemptions and 1.6% had moral/philosophical exemptions, while 1.4% were noncompliant but still attending school. Measles cases continue to grow, sparking debate among Americans on vaccines 1 of 11 Instructions for a Measles vaccination is seen outside of the Lubbock Public Health facility on April 9, 2025 in Lubbock, Texas. The city of Lubbock has confirmed a second measles related death amidst an ongoing outbreak which began in late January. As of early April, the Texas Department of State Health Services have confirmed over 500 cases, within 22 counties, ranging from the South Plains toward the Panhandle. (Brandon Bell, Getty Images) More The percentage of kids entering kindergarten fully vaccinated was lower than the overall rate, with only 91.8% of students in that age range coming to school with all required vaccines. That population did not exceed 95% for any required vaccine except hepatitis B. Here's a breakdown of the percentage of kindergarteners who were fully vaccinated: Varicella-Zoster Virus: 92.9% Private/independent and public schools had higher rates of vaccinations among kindergarteners (above 93% for all vaccines), while religious schools saw the lowest rates of vaccinations, with no rates above 90% for all vaccines. Overall, 60.5% of schools had a student population that was at least 95% fully vaccinated, with public schools reporting the highest percentage of these schools at 69.6%, followed by private/independent schools, then charter schools. Religious schools had the lowest percentage at just 31.4%. Have student vaccination rates declined in Pittsburgh? When more than 95% of a community is vaccinated against measles, that community has achieved herd immunity, meaning most people are protected against the disease, according to the Centers for Disease Control . Kindergarteners in Allegheny County have been below that threshold for several years, according to state records . Here's how overall vaccination rates have dropped among kindergarteners in Allegheny County: How many cases of measles have there been in Pennsylvania, US this year? There have been 232 reported cases of measles in Pennsylvania as of Aug. 10, when the most recent update to Pennsylvania Department of Health's dashboard happened. Thirty-eight people have been hospitalized. All cases were among people who were not fully vaccinated. Nationwide, there were 2,465 confirmed cases of measles, according to the CDC . The agency noted that it was aware of probable measles cases but that unconfirmed cases were not included in its data. Ninety-three percent of those cases occurred in people who were unvaccinated or who had an unknown vaccination status. Meanwhile, 3% of people with measles had received one MMR dose, while 4% were fully vaccinated. Nearly half of cases (1,189 or 48%) were among people age 5 to 19. How well does measles vaccine protect against infection, hospitalization, death? Two doses of the MMR vaccine provide 97% protection against the virus, according to the CDC , with children usually receiving their first dose at 12 to 15 months and a second at four to six years. It's estimated that one in five people who aren't vaccinated and get measles will need to be hospitalized, according to the CDC. Health experts have emphasized that the best protection against the disease is the vaccine, which can be given by itself, as part of an MMR vaccine or as part of the measles-mumps-rubella-varicella (MMRV) shot. How does measles spread? Measles is an airborne disease, which means that it spreads when an infected person exhales, coughs or sneezes, according to the World Health Organization . It can remain in the air for two hours after the infected person has left the area, and droplets can remain infectious on surfaces. A person with measles is contagious four days before the development of a rash to four days after the rash erupts, according to the WHO . What are the symptoms of measles? Signs of a measles infection generally appear seven to 14 days after someone encounters the virus. The following symptoms may be observed, according to the CDC : Koplik spots (white spots inside the mouth) Rash that generally appears three to five days after the first symptoms, beginning as flat red spots on the face and hairline before spreading downward on the body Some people develop complications from measles. Complications may include: Encephalitis, which can lead to convulsions, deafness or intellectual disability Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a fatal disease of the nervous system Pregnancy complications, which may include premature birth or a low-birth-weight baby This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: As measles cases continue to surge, are Pittsburgh schools prepared?

content_title: Ohio measles outbreak cases rise again, surpass last year's numbers
content: News Sports Business Opinion Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTHCARE Ohio measles outbreak cases rise again, surpass last year's numbers Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Aug. 13, 2026, 3:17 p.m. ET Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026 continues to grow, spreading to another county and surpassing the total number of cases from 2025 at the last count. Harrison County Public Health reported a measles case there on Aug. 12. Statewide, the Ohio Department of Health is reporting 69 cases in 11 counties, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Aug. 13. That's up from 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Nationwide, measles cases nationwide hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. Data released July 22 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 2,295 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991. Measles growing in Ohio; counties reporting cases Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashtabula: 17 Cuyahoga: 3 Franklin: 7 Geauga: 16 Harrison: 3 Holmes: 2 Knox: 1 Ottawa: 1 Trumbull: 2 Tuscarawas: 8 Wayne: 2 Unknown: 7 The latest case count reflects two previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with 45 in 2025, seven cases in 2024 and one case in 2023. Where are measles cases spreading? While Harrison County Public Health reported one case of measles as of Aug. 7, the state dashboard shows two additional cases there. The Wayne County Health Department reports some of its cases are likely associated with a previously identified measles exposure event at Smokey Lane Stables, 686 Smokey Lane Road NW in Sugarcreek, on July 17. One of the Tuscarawas cases is from the same event, that health department reports. Geauga Public Health reports that the individuals with measles visited several locations while able to spread the virus, including Bloomfield Horse Sale, 2211 Kinsman Road NW, on July 18. The Tuscarawas health department reports that another of its cases was exposed at the Bloomfield Livestock Auction, at the same address as Bloomfield Horse Sale, on on the same day. In Trumbull County, health officials report that infected individuals were at the Walmart in Liberty on July 29 and Akron Children's Mahoning Valley Emergency Department in Boardman on Aug. 2, during the time they were able to spread the virus. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. Why are measles cases on the rise? Ohio vaccination rates Vaccination for measles has declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventives, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine ahead of back-to-school season. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023, the most recent year available from ODH. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Trump signs executive order to separate MMR vaccine President Donald Trump signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, USA TODAY reports. "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lowers overall vaccination rates, according to experts. Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before, through four days after, a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. USA TODAY reporters James Powel and Mary Walrath-Holdridge contributed to this report. Featured Weekly Ad

content: News Sports Business Data Real Estate Obituaries eNewspaper Legals PUBLIC SAFETY One case of measles confirmed in Tioga County Jillian McCarthy Binghamton Press & Sun Bulletin Updated Aug. 14, 2026, 12:06 p.m. ET One case of measles has been confirmed in Tioga County. In a statement on Aug. 14, Tioga County Public Health announced an investigation into one confirmed case of measles in an unvaccinated county resident. Measles, a viral illness spread through coughing and sneezing, can remain alive and infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person has left the room, according to county public health. As part of the investigation, county public health officials are conducting contact tracing. They have successfully identified and are directly contacting all individuals known to have been exposed. An individual who has measles is contagious four days prior to a rash beginning and four days after the rash appears. Symptoms of measles typically begin between seven and 14 days after exposure to the virus and nine out of 10 unvaccinated people who are exposed to the virus will contract it. So far in 2026, there have been six confirmed cases of measles in New York City and 12 elsewhere in New York for 18 total cases as of Aug. 14, according to the New York State Department of Health. How to stay safe The overall risk of measles to the general public remains low, particularly for individuals who are fully vaccinated against the disease, according to county public health. Measles, however, is extremely contagious, and anyone unvaccinated, pregnant, under 12 months of age or immunocompromised is at a higher risk and should talk with their health care provider. If you were exposed or you think you may have been exposed, it's recommended to monitor you and your family members for symptoms. Early symptoms will typically appear between seven and 14 days after exposure and can include a high fever, often rising to about 101 degrees, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. A red, blotchy rash typically appears three to five days after initial symptoms begin, usually starting on the face along the hairline and spreading downward to the rest of the body, according to the county public health. If you are seeking medical attention, do not walk into a clinic, urgent care or emergency room without calling ahead. Inform them that you may have been exposed to measles ahead of time — this allows health care facilities to take precautions such as placing you in an isolated room to prevent spreading the virus to other vulnerable patients in the waiting room or other areas. Tioga County Public Health is asking anyone with questions to call 607-687-8600 or visit ph.tiogacountyny.gov.
